goal: A browser game of Tetris that a person can actually sit down and play. Pieces fall and can be moved, rotated and dropped; filled lines clear and score; the game speeds up and eventually ends. It should be clear at a glance what is happening and what is coming next. It runs by opening one HTML file, is controlled from the keyboard, and feels responsive rather than sluggish.

history.why: Both artifacts keep the controlled piece legal (no overlap/out-of-bounds) in every trial I ran: wall-hugging left/right, rotating flush against each wall, and hard-dropping repeatedly across ~15 runs covering all 7 piece types (verified visually via play.mjs screenshots, and for the simpler artifact also verified programmatically — I injected a script that rotated every piece type through 6 states and confirmed cell-count integrity and correct cycle periods, since its game state happens to be globally accessible in the page). Where they differ is the sophistication of the actual mechanic being judged. Artifact A (doc-2.html) implements real SRS: separate 5-offset kick tables for I vs JLSTZ pieces, separate tables for CW vs CCW rotation (KICK_JLSTZ, KICK_JLSTZ_CCW, KICK_I, KICK_I_CCW), a lock-delay window before a grounded piece merges, and DAS-tuned auto-repeat for left/right that scales with level. Artifact B (doc-1.html) rotates every piece with a single hard-coded list of 14 [dx,dy] kick offsets (KICKS) tried in the same fixed order regardless of piece shape or rotation direction, supports only one rotation direction (no CCW), and has no lock delay at all — the instant a piece can't move down further it merges into the board on the very next gravity/down-key check, giving no adjustment window once grounded. Both 'work' in the sense of never producing an illegal board state in my tests, but A's rotation/kick/lock-delay system is the standards-correct, piece-aware implementation the goal's 'moved, rotated, and dropped... feels responsive' bar implies, while B's is a functional but generic approximation.

built.changed:
In /tmp/gauntlet-tetris-1788004251/doc-1.html:

1. Kick tables: replaced the single flat 14-entry KICKS array used for every piece and only-CW rotation with three piece-specific SRS-style kick tables (KICKS_JLSTZ, KICKS_I, KICKS_O), each indexed by rotation-state transition key ("0>1", "1>0", "1>2", ... covering all 8 CW/CCW transitions around the 4-state cycle). Each piece object now carries a rotation-state field `r` (0-3) and a type field `t` (0-6, matching SHAPES order I,O,T,J,L,S,Z). kickTableFor(pieceType) selects the I table for the I piece, the O table (all zero offsets) for O, and the JLSTZ table for the rest.

2. Rotation direction: rotate() became rotate(dir), with rotateCW() and rotateCCW() matrix helpers. Bound Up/X to CW and Z to CCW in the keydown handler (previously only CW/ArrowUp existed). The on-page instructions line was updated to mention both keys.

3. Lock delay: renamed merge() to lockPiece() (kept as the merge/board-write/line-clear/respawn function, unchanged internally). Added a grounded() helper, a lockStart/lockResets pair of state variables, and LOCK_DELAY=500ms / MAX_LOCK_RESETS=15 constants. The rAF loop no longer calls lockPiece the instant the piece can't fall: when grounded() it starts a timer and only calls lockPiece() once LOCK_DELAY has elapsed (or the reset budget is exhausted); while airborne it clears the timer and advances gravity by dropMs as before. move() and rotate() call refreshLock(), which restarts the timer (up to the reset cap) if the piece is still grounded after the move/rotation succeeds, so a last-moment slide or spin under a landed piece still counts. Hard drop (hard()) still locks instantly, as does pressing the soft-drop key while already grounded (down() now calls lockPiece() directly in that case) — those two paths were left as immediate locks since the gap was specifically about lockPiece merging with no grace window on ordinary landing, not about hard/soft-drop semantics.

Verified with node by extracting and eval'ing the inline script: all 7 piece types run 4 CW + 4 CCW rotations in open space without exceptions and return to rotation-state 0; a piece placed on a flat obstruction locks at simulated t=512ms rather than instantly at t=0.

regression.why:
Both artifacts run cleanly (verified with headless play.mjs — no page errors on either), share identical board/line-clear/scoring/speed-up code, and both omit a next-piece preview, so that part of the goal is an equal weakness on both sides, not a differentiator. Where they diverge is core piece-control quality, and I traced the actual mechanics in both files (doc-1.snapshot-round.html = A, doc-1.html = B) rather than just eyeballing screenshots, since screenshots of a randomized game aren't directly comparable run to run.

A's rotate() applies one flat, position-only wall-kick offset list to every piece type and every rotation transition, and its lock behavior is entirely tied to the gravity tick: down() merges the piece into the board the instant it is grounded, whether that call comes from the auto-drop timer or the player's own ArrowDown press. Because the auto-drop interval (dropMs) is exactly what the goal requires to shrink over time ('the game speeds up'), the player's practical window to nudge or rotate a piece after it touches down shrinks in lockstep with difficulty, from ~700ms down to ~120ms.

B implements piece-type- and rotation-state-specific SRS-style kick tables (separate tables for I, O, and JLSTZ pieces, indexed by the exact 'from>to' transition) plus an independent lock-delay system (fixed 500ms grace window with a capped 15-reset budget from further moves/rotations) that is decoupled from dropMs. That means B's maneuverability at the bottom of the well stays constant as the game accelerates, while A's degrades toward instant-lock — directly undercutting the goal's explicit 'feels responsive rather than sluggish' requirement at exactly the moment (higher speed / later game) it matters most. This is the single largest, concretely fixable gap: A needs a drop-speed-independent lock-delay grace window (and ideally per-piece kick tables) so late-game play doesn't become a snap-lock trap.

history.why: Both artifacts implement genuinely correct SRS-style collision/kick tables and pass every wall-hug/rotate/drop probe I ran with no illegal or overlapping placements. I verified this by driving both through the exact test sequence (adjusted only to first press Space to leave doc-2's start menu, since ArrowLeft/Right are repurposed as a level selector before the game starts) and dumping the live canvas as a text grid at each stage via CDP Runtime.evaluate, rather than eyeballing screenshots. Artifact A's piece (random per run, e.g. an S/Z) moved flush to the left wall on 5x ArrowLeft, rotated in place with a legal kick, moved flush to the right wall (touching column 9) on 7x ArrowRight, rotated again near that wall without going out of bounds, soft-dropped 2 rows on 2x ArrowDown, and hard-dropped to lock exactly where its own ghost predicted — no overlap, no clipping. Artifact B (an S-piece in my trace, an I-piece in another) showed the identical pattern: flush-left clamp, legal in-place rotation, flush/near-flush right clamp, correct discrete down-steps, correct hard-drop lock. Reading both kick tables against the canonical SRS I-piece offsets confirms both are mathematically correct (just applying the canvas +y-down flip differently: B pre-bakes the sign flip into its table, A flips the sign at application time with `currentY -= ky`). So on raw legality, they tie. The separator is movement feel: A implements a real DAS/ARR system (`startDAS`/`stopDAS`, `getDASDelay`/`getDASRepeat`) that fires the first move immediately on keydown and then auto-repeats at a tuned interval that gets faster as level increases (170ms→100ms delay, 50ms→30ms repeat) — plus a ghost piece that previews the exact hard-drop landing square. B has no keyup handler and no repeat logic of any kind (`grep -n "keyup|setInterval|repeat|DAS" doc-1.html` returns nothing) — holding a direction key relies entirely on the browser/OS's native, untuned key-repeat, which is not scaled to the game's speed and is the kind of thing that reads as "sluggish" under sustained input, which the goal explicitly calls out.
history.gap: B has no custom auto-repeat (DAS/ARR) for held movement keys — its keydown handler calls move(-1)/move(1) once per event with no keyup tracking or interval-based repeat, so continuous left/right motion is entirely at the mercy of the browser's native OS key-repeat timing (untuned, inconsistent across platforms, not scaled to game speed). A implements a proper delayed-auto-shift system that moves immediately on press and then auto-repeats at a level-scaled interval. This is the single largest thing separating them on movement responsiveness specifically, since correctness/legality of collision and kicks is otherwise a tie.

The one place they diverge is soft drop: doc-1's ArrowDown calls down() synchronously in the keydown handler, so every press is guaranteed to move the piece exactly one row (or lock it if grounded) regardless of frame timing. doc-2's ArrowDown only sets a `keys['down']` flag; the actual row-advance happens later inside the rAF loop's `while (dropTimer >= dropInterval && !onGround)` using a dropTimer that is shared with ambient gravity and carries state across frames — so whether a given press produces 0, 1, or several rows depends on how much gravity time had already accumulated when the key arrived, not on the press itself. That inconsistency is visible in doc-2's own code: left/right/rotate are all 'act immediately on keydown', but down is the one control that is not, breaking the pattern the game itself otherwise follows.
positions.gap: doc-2's soft drop (ArrowDown) does not guarantee a deterministic one-row response per keypress the way left/right/rotate do in the same file — it sets a `keys['down']` flag that is only consumed by the shared gravity accumulator (`dropTimer`) on the next animation frame(s), so the number of rows a single tap produces depends on how much ambient gravity time had already accumulated, not on the press itself. Bind ArrowDown's keydown handler to call a synchronous single-row moveDown()-and-relock-check (mirroring how doc-1's down() works, or how doc-2 already treats moveLeft/moveRight/rotate) so every soft-drop press is a guaranteed, predictable step, and keep the held-key acceleration (the `keys['down']` flag) purely as a secondary continuous-hold effect layered on top.

goal_coupling.reasoning:
The artifact (doc-1.html) is a self-contained single-file browser Tetris implementation: a canvas board (10x20 grid at S=24px cell size), seven SHAPES, a KICKS table for rotation, keydown handling for ArrowLeft/ArrowRight/ArrowUp/ArrowDown/Space, a merge() function that clears full rows and adds to score, and a dropMs value that decreases as score rises (game speeds up) until `over` is set and "Game Over" is drawn.

Checking each goal clause against the artifact's own wording:

- "A browser game of Tetris" — the artifact's <title> is "Tetris"; this is just the subject name, not a distinctive coinage.
- "Pieces fall and can be moved, rotated and dropped" — the artifact's on-page instruction text reads "Arrows move and rotate, Down drops faster, Space drops hard." Both texts use the verbs move/rotate/drop, but these are the standard, unavoidable vocabulary for describing Tetris controls (any Tetris document would use them), not an unusual phrase coined by this artifact.
- "filled lines clear and score" — the artifact's merge() clears rows where `board[r].every(v=>v)` and increments `score`; again this is the genre's own vocabulary (line-clear, score) rather than a distinctive artifact detail. The goal does not mention the artifact's specific score table `[0,100,300,500,800]` or the `Score ` text prefix.
- "the game speeds up and eventually ends" — the artifact does compute `dropMs = Math.max(120, 700 - Math.floor(score/500)*60)` and sets `over=true`/draws "Game Over", but the goal names no specific numbers (120, 700, 60, 500) or the literal string "Game Over" — it stays at the generic "speeds up"/"ends" level.
- "clear at a glance what is happening and what is coming next" — the artifact has no next-piece preview at all (only `#score` div and the single canvas showing the falling piece); this clause names a feature this artifact never attempts, so it cannot be read off the artifact's visible features.
- "runs by opening one HTML file" — true of the artifact (single .html with inline <style>/<script>), but this is a generic requirement any single-file HTML game meets, not distinctive artifact vocabulary.
- "controlled from the keyboard" — matches the artifact's `addEventListener('keydown', ...)`, again a generic description of the mechanism rather than a name or number pulled from the file.
- "feels responsive rather than sluggish" — subjective language with no counterpart in the artifact's text at all.

No goal clause uses a number, identifier, or coined term that is unique to this file (e.g., `KICKS`, `dropMs`, `S=24`, `C=10`, `R=20`, the specific score table, the canvas pixel dimensions, or the literal "Game Over" string). goal_fairness.reference_is_for: This is a fully implemented browser Tetris game. The file title is "Tetris" and its meta description reads "A free, open-source Tetris game you can play right in your browser." It has a canvas-based board (`#board`, 300x600 with a 10x20 grid at BLOCK=30), tetromino SHAPES for I/O/T/S/Z/J/L pieces with SRS wall-kick rotation tables, a 7-bag randomizer, a `Next` preview canvas and a `Hold` canvas, ghost-piece rendering, line-clear detection (`clearLines`) with scoring (`LINE_SCORES`), a level/speed curve (`LEVEL_SPEEDS` array from 800ms down to 33ms per drop, tied to `level = Math.floor(lines/10)+1`), a `triggerGameOver` function with high-score persistence via localStorage, and a keyboard control scheme documented in the visible Controls panel (arrows/WASD for move, down/S for soft drop, Space for hard drop, up/W/X and Z for rotate CW/CCW, C/Shift for hold, Esc/M for menu). Performance optimizations (pre-rendered sprites, cached board canvas, requestAnimationFrame loop) target responsiveness. It is delivered as a single HTML file with all game logic inline in `<script>` tags (external assets like audio/icons are decorative extras, not required for core play).

THERE IS NO RATCHET; REGRESSIONS ARE MEASURED AND NOT REVERTED (issue #18). A ratchet keeps the best version and restores it — nothing here does that, and the field is called `regression` rather than `ratchet` so a record cannot imply otherwise. Each built round asks one fresh critic which is closer to the goal — the version this round produced, or the copy taken before it — and the answer is recorded per round as `regression`, with `regressed: true` on any round the critic judged worse than what it replaced. Nothing is rolled back, and the reason has changed since this sentence was first written: the detection rate behind it was one observation, and is now 12/15 with a 95% interval of 55%-93% (docs/runs/2026-08-27-detection-rate/verdict.md). What remains is that the interval is wide, the trials differ by one mechanical transform, and every miss was a defect of 3 bytes or fewer - so an automatic revert would act on a judgement measured on nothing like the case it would decide. A wrong revert is also quieter than a wrong refusal, which at least stops the run loudly. The previous version is named in the record, so a regression is recoverable by hand. What this still cannot do: VERIFY the snapshot — a Workflow script has no filesystem, so the copy is the builder's word, exactly as sizes are the breaker's — and tell an improvement from a lateral move, since one judge on one day is the whole of the comparison. A round whose builder reported no snapshot says so in `regression_why_not` rather than reading as a round that was checked and found fine.

THE BLINDNESS PROBE MODELS THE FILESYSTEM ONLY, and the critic and builder both hold WebSearch and WebFetch. The probe resolves an artifact's citations against this working tree, so a `clean` verdict means neither artifact gives away its origin TO A READER OF THIS DISK. It says nothing about the network: a reference with a published copy can be fetched and compared, which identifies which side is the shipped one, and a builder can retrieve a fix from the web rather than composing it — a live retrieval channel distinct both from the model's own prior and from anything on disk, and the one issue #25 does not cover. Neither agent needs the network for its stated job.

The critic holds Bash and KillShell, which can write files directly (redirection, heredocs, etc.) — nothing mechanically stops it from altering either artifact through Bash instead of Write/Edit. The no-Write/no-Edit property above is real but narrow (prompt-deep, not structural).
AB_SCHEMA.gap is a free-text string: nothing stops several gaps being packed into it (e.g. "Gap 1: ... Gap 2: ..."). Only one gap SLOT is enforced, not one gap.
Nothing verifies that the named gap is really the LARGEST — only that exactly one slot came back.

NO CALIBRATION ANYWHERE. Nothing in this plugin checks that a critic could have failed — no defect is planted, no control is run on a clean copy, and a critic that approves everything is indistinguishable from a critic that is right. The seeded-defect machinery that used to do this lived in the review panel and was deleted with it; this is now the plugin's largest unmeasured property, not a lane that exists elsewhere.

The breaker is checked at ROUND BOUNDARIES, not continuously. Removing the token while a critic or builder is mid-flight does not abort that agent — the run stops before the next round starts. To stop a round already in progress, kill the workflow itself.
Nothing stops the token being re-created after a cancel. The breaker reports the state at each boundary; it does not latch.

With no budget target set, there is no pre-committed ceiling at all — the run continues until it wins, an agent fails, or the operator cancels. That is the source design rather than an oversight — it says "there should be no arbitrary final round" — and it means an unattended run is bounded only by the host's own runaway backstop.

split_check.why_not: the run never reached WON, so no winning split existed to falsify — this check only runs after every piece has beaten the reference

reading_note: Stopping on CANCELLED or BUDGET is not failure. The source is explicit that a hard bar "does not need to be realistically reachable" and that the operator stopping is the normal ending — Shumer stopped his own run "while it was still improving". Read `gaps_in_order` instead: if the gaps got smaller and more specific, the loop was working. If the last round names the same gap as the first, it was not — and that is the signal to read, not the verdict.
